https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c235.text: Figure caption, "I think there's a deal" - Trump on calling off Iran strikes By Bernd Debusmann Jr ,Â White House reporter ,Â Reporting from Air Force One Â and Â James Chater Published 3 August 2026, 01:11 BST Updated 7 minutes ago Iran says it is negotiating with Oman to reach "an understanding" over a temporary route through the Strait of Hormuz to allow commercial shipping to resume. The statement came after US President Donald Trump said new talks on ending the war in Iran would begin on Monday - and that he had called off "massive" strikes on the country for this purpose. Trump did not specify who would take part in the talks. Earlier he had said the "perimeters" of a deal had been agreed - and would include reopening Hormuz, the vital waterway whose closure by Iran has sent oil prices soaring. In its response, Iran said it was not negotiating with the US - and had no plans to do so. Foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei added that Tehran was negotiating with Oman to reach "an understanding over a path to ensure the security of shipping passage through the Strait of Hormuz". Tehran has repeatedly closed off the strait since the US and Israel started attacks on the country in February. Talks to end the conflict - mostly facilitated by mediators - collapsed last month, ending a ceasefire agreed in April. Trump has repeatedly vowed that a negotiated end to the war is near, only for tit-for-tat strikes to resume. Speaking on board Air Force One on Sunday, he said Iran "knew the extent" of the planned US strikes "because they saw it forming", adding: "We're talking to them in the form of a negotiation. It begins tomorrow afternoon." Trump declined to outline a deadline for a deal to be struck with Tehran, adding: "We'll just see how it is. We're ready to go anytime we want... I'm not looking to kill people." Trump added that Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman - as well as US partners such as the United Arab Emirates and Qatar - had urged him against conducting strikes over the weekend. "We were all set to go," Trump said. "The reason they asked is [that] they think there's a deal," he said. "There's a deal on Hormuz, and there will be a deal on the nuclear." Global oil prices fell on Monday morning in Asia trading after Trump's announcement. Brent Crude oil was down by 4.5% at $83.98 (Â£62.26), while US-traded oil was 4.6% lower at $80.74 (Â£59.85). Energy prices have fluctuated since the conflict started on 28 February as traders reacted to disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Around 20% of the world's crude oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) usually flows through the strait. Vessel-tracking data from trade intelligence company Kpler suggests commercial shipping through the strait has slowed. According to the data, 51 vessel crossings occurred through the strait between 30 July and 2 August. This is a drop of around 28% compared to the previous 4 days, in which 71 crossings were recorded through the strait. Iran's semi-official Mehr news agency denied that Tehran had asked the US to hold off on further military action, saying Trump's claims were "nothing but a new lie". During his remarks on Air Force One, Trump said that the planned strikes would have been "the biggest attack since World War Two", and could have derailed prospects of a negotiated end to the months-long war. Trump declined to answer if he had been planning to strike Iranian energy infrastructure, which international law experts have said could constitute a war crime . Back on 7 April, the US president warned that "a whole civilisation will die tonight" if Iran refused to engage in peace talks. That threat did result in historic face-to-face talks in Pakistan, led by Vice-President JD Vance. However, those negotiations did not result in a deal. The Trump administration has also been largely dismissive of data showing the war - and its economic impact - are broadly unpopular with Americans, including with many Republicans. Polls showing widespread dissatisfaction with the handling of the war have prompted alarm among some conservative strategists ahead of the coming November midterms. https://www.politico.eu/article/france-n.text: PARIS — France is not yet ready to face cheap, mass-produced threats like drones, the country's chief of defense staff, Gen. Fabien Mandon, warned Wednesday. Defending in a financially sustainable manner against low-cost weapons manufactured in bulk, including Iranian-made Shahed drones, has been one of the main challenges for Western armed forces since the war in Ukraine started. "We have enemies who have developed a large number of low-cost solutions that will wear down our models," Mandon said at an event organized by France's main business lobby Medef. "We’re not there yet. It’s nothing catastrophic, we’re still at peace. But we need to make this move." Advertisement Advertisement NATO arsenals have long been composed of high-tech, sophisticated missiles worth several million dollars each, which land forces, navies and warplanes have been firing against unmanned aerial vehicles worth just tens of thousands of dollars. Now, the main goal is to significantly reduce the so-called cost per kill, meaning how much money has been spent to neutralize a threat. Most recently, the French air force used costly missiles against cheap Iranian drones sent toward Gulf countries. French legacy arms companies such as MBDA, as well as startups including Alta Ares and Harmattan AI, are working on lower-cost, mass-producible weapons to counter such threats. "Our defensive weapons are not produced in sufficient quantities to stop these waves of saturation," the French general said. He added that he was working to accelerate the French armed forces' use of drones. Defense companies "have to be hungry and adaptable in a fast-paced world, where our competitors adapt quickly," Mandon told the audience. Advertisement Advertisement

Photograph: Michael Probst/AP Germany Officials urge calm after malaria outbreak kills two staff at Frankfurt airport Mosquito traps are set up at Germany’s biggest airport and doctors are asked to look out for symptoms of disease Kate Connolly in Berlin Thu 27 Aug 2026 11.23 EDT Last modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 11.42 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google German health officials are seeking to reassure the public after two workers at the country’s biggest airport died of malaria. Mosquito traps have been set up at Frankfurt airport and a mosquito monitoring process is under way. A detailed investigation is being conducted to clarify how the workers contracted the disease. Since last month, six people are known to have caught malaria tropica – the most dangerous form of the disease – in connection with their work at the airport. Of the two that have died, one began getting sick at the start of July and the other in mid-August. The four other people who were infected have been treated in hospital and are now out of danger, according to Frankfurt’s public health department. Letters have been sent to all airport workers to raise awareness about symptoms and urge vigilance. Doctors are being asked to watch out for patients with unexplained fever who work in and around the airport. In a statement on its website, the health department acknowledged the existence of “airport malaria”, where mosquitoes from malaria-endemic areas are transported in flight cabins or in baggage holds. View image in fullscreen A female Anopheles stephensi mosquito. The species has been linked to the Frankfurt malaria outbreak. Photograph: CDC/Phanie/Rex Features It said that because this was “a very rare occurrence”, malaria could easily be overlooked and diagnosis delayed, increasing the chance of death. It said human-to-human transmission was not possible. The Robert Koch Institute, which is responsible for disease control and prevention in Germany , believes the Frankfurt infection was transmitted by an Anopheles stephensi mosquito imported by plane. A spokesperson for Fraport, which operates the airport, confirmed that mosquito traps had been set up in and around the site and that mosquitoes had been caught. These are being examined in a tropical medicine laboratory in Antwerp, Belgium. Can you stop malaria crossing borders? One nation’s bid to wipe out the disease Read more Peter Tinnemann, the head of Frankfurt’s health department, told the broadcaster Hessische Rundfunk: “The mosquito is probably already dead.” He said higher temperatures in Germany increased the likelihood of mosquitoes surviving for extended periods but the risk to the population of Frankfurt was low. “Not everyone should assume that just because they have a headache, fever and nonspecific symptoms they are now infected with malaria because of the case at the airport,” he added. But he said the rise in malaria cases made it necessary to check whether existing measures, including the disinfection of aircraft and removing breeding grounds for mosquitoes, were being correctly followed. A study that set out to record all cases of airport and baggage malaria in Europe from 1969 to 2024 found 145 instances, nine of them in Germany. The Robert Koch Institute said Germany’s last outbreak of airport malaria was also at Frankfurt, in 2023, when a single documented infection was successfully treated. About 90% of all malaria cases occur in sub-Saharan Africa. Countries from this region with direct flight connections to Frankfurt include Ethiopia, Kenya, Nigeria and Tanzania, all of which have a high to widespread malaria risk. Namibia and South Africa also have direct flights but are considered to be moderate to low risk. A mostani beruházás egy átfogó, 1,6 milliárd dolláros modernizációs program része, amelynek keretében a következő évtizedben több mint huszonnégy építési és felújítási projekt valósul meg a bázison. Robert Sturgill Jr. ezredes, a bázis és a 7. Bombázóezred parancsnoka a jövőbeli B-21-es komplexum idegközpontjaként jellemezte az épületet. Kiemelte, hogy a létesítmény legfontosabb elemei a korszerű kommunikációs hálózatok és a szigorú biztonsági rendszerek lesznek. A gépek fizikai elhelyezésén túl ugyanis a hajózószemélyzetnek és a támogató állománynak is szüksége van egy védett helyre a szigorúan titkos hadműveleti adatok kezeléséhez. A fejlesztéssel a Dyess légibázis egy lépéssel közelebb került ahhoz, hogy a B-21-esek harmadik fő üzemeltetési bázisává váljon. A légierő korábban már kijelölte a típus állomáshelyeit, így a texasi támaszpont a dél-dakotai Ellsworth és a Missouri állambeli Whiteman légibázisokhoz csatlakozik a programban. A hivatalos közlemény a bevetéstervező épület belső rendszereinek pontos részleteire, valamint a kivitelezés befejezésének és az átadásnak a dátumára nem tért ki.
